item.title: Optimal Signaling Mechanisms for One-round Matching Markets
item.description: arXiv:2611.31517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Signaling mechanisms are used in various types of matching markets so that applicants may credibly signal interest in firms. They have been observed to improve outcomes in job markets and dating markets, and proven to improve outcomes in several stylized theoretical models. In this paper we develop optimal signaling mechanisms for a simple one-round matching market consisting of $n$ applicants and $n$ firms. We consider a much richer space of signals than have been used previously, in theory or practice, and also consider randomized signaling mechanisms, which have not been systematically studied. For each $k \geq 1$, we determine the optimal deterministic and randomized signaling mechanisms in which applicants signal $k$ firms. In the limit as $k\to \infty$, our deterministic mechanism guarantees that in expectation, $\approx 75.4504\%$ of the applicants receive job offers, and this is optimal. Likewise, for $k \to \infty$, our randomized mechanism guarantees that $\approx 78.197\%$ of the applicants receive offers, which is also optimal. The optimal $k$-signal randomized mechanism is non-constructive, and has a rather complex description. We describe some simple randomized signaling mechanisms whose efficiency surpasses that of the limiting optimal deterministic mechanism. Finally, we also discuss incentive-compatibility for the firms to follow the mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Varsha Dani, David G. Harris, Thomas P. Hayes, Seth Pettie

item.title: Collateral Architecture and Correlated Slashing in Liquid Restaking
item.description: arXiv:2611.31700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liquid restaking protocols allow pooled stake to support multiple slashable commitments, creating an allocation problem in which additional rewards must be balanced against correlated slash claims. This risk depends not only on dependence between slash events, but also on how collateral is allocated or reused across commitments. We develop a unified model ranging from unique stake, where capital is divided among positions, to shared collateral, where the same capital supports multiple commitments. We show that portfolio variance is governed jointly by gross exposure, exposure concentration, and failure dependence. Spreading fixed capital reduces risk toward a correlation-dependent floor, whereas repeatedly pledging the same collateral can make risk grow quadratically with breadth. We then study risk-sensitive allocators competing for fixed reward pools distributed proportionally to committed exposure. A single allocator has a unique optimum, and in a symmetric benchmark greater risk sensitivity encourages diversification under unique stake but discourages additional commitments under shared collateral. With multiple allocators, positive background stake guarantees a unique pure Nash equilibrium and supports a globally convergent projected method. Reproducible synthetic stress tests support these mechanisms. In the strongest common-factor environment, relaxing the reuse cap raises equilibrium reward by 2.47 times but aggregate 99% conditional value at risk by 3.77 times. Competition creates overexposure relative to a planner, while ignoring covariance raises true variance by 6.3%. The results provide a unified framework for collateral reuse, correlated operational risk, and incentive design in decentralized security markets.
item.dc:creator: Zhejun Zhang, Justin Cho, Francisco Marmolejo-Coss\'io

item.title: Query-Sample Tradeoffs for Revenue Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2611.31982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce and study the full query-sample tradeoff for revenue maximization with a single buyer whose value follows an unknown distribution. A learner may adaptively combine value samples, which reveal full buyer values, with pricing queries, which reveal only whether a fresh buyer accepts a selected price. The goal is to learn a price that achieves a $(1-\varepsilon)$-multiplicative approximation to optimal revenue with high probability. We ask when, and by how much, reducing the sample budget increases the number of pricing queries required. We establish tight tradeoff bounds for monotone-hazard-rate (MHR), regular, and quasi-monotone-hazard-rate (quasi-MHR) distributions, and almost tight bounds for quasi-regular distributions. Our results reveal sharply different benefits from combining the two information sources. Quasi-MHR distributions admit a smooth intermediate tradeoff: additional samples can reduce the query requirement by polynomial factors. For MHR and regular distributions, however, a sufficiently small constant fraction of the sample-only requirement still leaves the learner facing the full asymptotic query cost attainable with one sample. Our upper bounds are achieved by algorithms that collect all value samples before making queries, while our lower bounds hold even under arbitrary adaptive interleaving of the two forms of access. Along the way, we also fully characterize the sample-only and single-sample query complexities for all four families, eliminating the extra logarithmic dependence on $1/\varepsilon$ in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Yaonan Jin, Wei Tang, Yifan Wang, Mengxiao Zhang

item.title: Approximate MMS allocations for large number of agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.33051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider allocation of indivisible items to agents with non-negative additive valuations, under the maximin share (MMS) fairness benchmark. We prove that for every $\rho < 1$, there exists some $n_{\rho}$ such that every allocation instance with $n \ge n_{\rho}$ agents has a $\rho$-MMS allocation. This was explicitly stated as a conjecture in a recent paper of the authors, where it was shown to hold if the number of items is at most $(2 - \epsilon)n$ (and $n \ge n_{\rho, \epsilon}$). We build on some techniques from that earlier paper, including the construction of $\textit{ordinal MMS}$ allocations that give $n - O(\log^2 n)$ agents their full MMS. Among the new techniques that we introduce is the definition of $\textit{block-matchings}$ between the MMS partitions of two agents, and a proof that if the number of item types is small, then block-matchings of small width necessarily exist.
item.dc:creator: Uriel Feige, Vadim Grinberg

item.title: $(1-\varepsilon)$-MMS Allocations
item.description: arXiv:2611.33052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study maximin share (MMS) allocations of $m$ indivisible items among $n$ agents with additive valuations. We prove that for both goods and chores, the optimal MMS approximation factor converges to $1$ as $n$ grows. In particular, for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, sufficiently large $n$, and any $m$, we give polynomial-time algorithms that compute a $(1-\varepsilon)$-MMS allocation for goods and a $(1+\varepsilon)$-MMS allocation for chores. Furthermore, both algorithms can be implemented using a polynomial number of bundle comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Zehan Lin, Shengxin Liu, Biaoshuai Tao, Xiaowei Wu, Yuhao Zhang

item.title: Breaking the Square-Root Barrier for Linear Swap Regret in Polyhedral Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.33081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study linear swap regret in self-play against all affine self-maps of each player's strategy polytope. Efficient adversarial bounds for this class scale as $\sqrt{T}$. On compact polytopes given by linear inequalities, our deterministic uncoupled dynamics achieve $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{poly}(D)T^{1/3})$ cumulative regret, where $D$ is the binary length of the game description. The bound is independent of the number of vertices. In perfect-recall $n$-player extensive-form games with at most $M$ terminal sequences per player, we obtain $\mathcal{O}(n^2M^4\log T)$ regret against all linear deviations, extending the logarithmic trigger-regret bound of Anagnostides, Farina, and Sandholm [AFS23]. This class can strictly contain the trigger deviations [FP23] and consists exactly of the deviations implementable by untimed communication (UTC), in which a player interleaves moves with mediator queries along a separate feasible path [ZFS24]. The proof combines optimistic log-barrier learning on a compact matrix lift with stability of the Gordon fixed point, using treeplex geometry in extensive form.
item.dc:creator: Vasilis Pollatos, Alberto Marchesi

item.title: Improved Downward-Closed Delegation Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2611.33095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study delegated choice under a downward-closed feasibility constraint, where the principal and agent values of each item may be arbitrarily correlated but items are independent. We give a deterministic, agent-oblivious menu that guarantees the principal more than $29/70\approx0.41429$ of the expected offline optimum under every best response, including ties resolved against the principal. The menu depends only on the feasible family and the principal's value distributions, and verifies a proposal using only its items and their principal values. The previous best guarantee for downward-closed constraints was $0.1098$. Matroid constraints admit a guarantee of one half, which is tight already in rank one, but downward-closed constraints do not: a five-item knapsack instance bounds every deterministic menu by $500/1011$ of the optimum, and no rule with randomized acceptance, even one that knows the agent's utilities, can guarantee more than $30/61$. An explicit computer-assisted family of instances lowers the bound to $0.48105$ for all such rules. The guarantee is proved by contradiction. If every menu in a fixed family earns at most a $29/70$ fraction of the optimum, then a normalized instance satisfies a finite system of affine inequalities among the survival functions, stop-loss transforms and overshoot means of its clipped optima. An exact rational certificate shows that the system is infeasible. We also give a short analytic proof that a single threshold on the reported total value guarantees $3/10$.
item.dc:creator: Hamed Abdi, Kiarash Banihashem, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Danny Mittal

item.title: Envy-Free Cake-Cutting for Five Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.33149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the envy-free cake-cutting problem, in which a divisible resource must be divided among a set of agents with heterogeneous preferences in a way that ensures that no agent envies the piece obtained by another. Remarkably, under some mild continuity assumptions on the agent valuations, it is known that an envy-free division where each agent receives a \emph{connected} piece of the cake is always guaranteed to exist. When the valuations are monotone, prior work has shown that a connected $\varepsilon$-envy-free division can be obtained using $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ queries for up to four agents, leaving the case of five or more agents open. In this work, we develop a new simpler approach that yields such an efficient algorithm for five agents. Our algorithm uses $\mathcal{O}(\log^3(1/\varepsilon))$ queries and also yields a novel proof of existence for five agents that does not rely on any fixed-point theorems beyond the intermediate value theorem.
item.dc:creator: Aris Filos-Ratsikas, Alexandros Hollender, Mohamad Latifian, Giannis Tyrovolas

item.title: Heterogeneous Risk-Sensitive Evolutionary Learning in Coordination Games: Polarization, Welfare Loss, and Intervention for Efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2611.31568v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study evolutionary learning in coordination games in a finite population of agents with heterogeneous risk attitudes, modeled using the entropic risk measure (ERM). The population consists of two subpopulations, each with a fixed risk attitude. Under risk-sensitive best response with mutations (BRM), we characterize the long-run outcomes of the learning process. In particular, we characterize when a polarized state, in which the two subpopulations choose different actions, is uniquely stochastically stable in terms of agents' risk attitudes and the subpopulation sizes. Notably, this polarized state is strictly Pareto dominated by the payoff-dominant equilibrium under both expected payoffs and agents' own ERM-adjusted payoffs. Moreover, its welfare, measured by average expected payoff, is always lower than that of the payoff-dominant equilibrium and can also be lower than that of the risk-dominant equilibrium. Thus, heterogeneity of risk attitudes in learning alone can lead to an inefficient long-run outcome. To mitigate such inefficiency, we propose intervention mechanisms to modify agents' risk attitudes in learning. We show that a sufficiently large intervention share (the fraction of agents modified) and sufficiently high intervention intensity (the increase in their risk parameter) ensure that the payoff-dominant equilibrium is uniquely stochastically stable. However, greater intervention intensity cannot compensate for an insufficient intervention share, and a larger intervention share cannot compensate for insufficient intervention intensity.
item.dc:creator: Solaleh Mohammadi, Yiman Fong, Kaiqing Zhang

item.title: A Constant-Factor Single-Sample Prophet Inequality for Subadditive Valuations
item.description: arXiv:2611.31685v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish a constant-factor single-sample prophet inequality for online combinatorial allocation with monotone subadditive valuations. Given one independent sample from each buyer's unknown distribution, our reduction converts any offline algorithm achieving an $\alpha$ fraction of optimal welfare into an online algorithm achieving an $\alpha/120$ fraction of the expected offline optimum. The guarantee holds for arbitrary arrival orders and extends to the stronger Game of Googol model. Our approach has two key ingredients: a prior-free random score generator and a new sample-based construction of tentative allocations. The tentative allocations capture substantial welfare while controlling contention for items, and the score generator relates itemwise competition in the tentative allocations to the value of retained bundles. The reduction is efficient whenever its offline allocator and score generator are efficient.
item.dc:creator: Shuchi Chawla, Trung Dang

item.title: An Order-Optimal Square-Root Bound for Online Maximin Share Allocation with Known Types
item.description: arXiv:2611.31732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An allocator knows the indivisible goods, the number $n$ of agents, and the $k$ possible additive valuations. Each agent reveals their type on arrival and must immediately receive an irrevocable bundle. Kulkarni, Mehta, and Shahkar established a deterministic guarantee of $1/k$ of maximin share (MMS) and an upper bound of $2/(\sqrt{k}-2)$ for $k>4$. We determine the optimal order $\Theta(k^{-1/2})$ by constructing a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, Single-or-Select. On every arrival sequence, it gives each agent a fraction $(1/\sqrt{2}-o(1))/\sqrt{k}$ of their truncated proportional share. This share dominates MMS and is the largest target $y$ for which the item values capped at $y$ sum to at least $ny$. By specializing the construction of Kulkarni et al. to two arrivals and counting its types exactly, we sharpen the upper bound to $(\sqrt{2}+o(1))/\sqrt{k}$ even for binary valuations. For two arrivals with binary valuations and every $k\ge2$, the optimal fraction is $1/p$, where $p$ is the largest integer with $1+\binom{2p}{2}\le k$. In particular, up to six binary types permit full maximin share. For two arbitrary additive types, a different polynomial-time algorithm guarantees $4/7$ of maximin share for any number of agents. This ratio is tight for the algorithm. With three arrivals and two types, the optimal deterministic fraction is exactly $9/10$. For randomized policies with $k$ known additive types, the optimal MMS fraction guaranteed to all agents with probability at least $1-\delta$ on every fixed arrival sequence is $\Theta(\max\{k^{-1/2},\sqrt{\delta}\})$ for $0\le\delta<1$.
item.dc:creator: Zheyu Zhou

item.title: The Oracle Is Not Enough: Secure Settlement for Prediction Markets
item.description: arXiv:2611.31866v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Prediction markets are becoming an important mechanism for aggregating information and forecasting uncertain real-world events. As they grow in scale and value, reliable settlement becomes critical because settlement determines the winning outcome and allocation of market collateral. Yet many heterogeneous markets require market-specific evidence and interpretation, and incorrect settlement can create direct financial incentives for manipulation. In this paper, we ask how to settle heterogeneous markets correctly and efficiently at scale. We first compare existing settlement designs in their support for heterogeneous markets, reliance on direct operator intervention, and resistance to manipulation, motivating a layered architecture that combines incentivized crowdsourcing with stake-backed voting and selective post-settlement review. Building on this architecture, we develop a stake-backed settlement protocol that provides economic security and settlement liveness under market-specific verification costs. Specifically, we prove that manipulation is unprofitable for every settled market and give two constructions that support sufficient self-enforcing participation with controlled reward expenditure. Using historical Polymarket and UMA data, we evaluate the protocol under real-world conditions. We find that 99% of admitted markets can be settled with modest participation rewards even under high verification costs.
item.dc:creator: Jiayu Liu, Sen Yang, Xueyuan Zhao, Kartik Nayak, Fan Zhang

item.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning via Monadic Continuations
item.description: arXiv:2611.32320v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Alpha-beta pruning is a fundamental technique in game-playing AI, enabling efficient minimax search by avoiding the exploration of branches that cannot affect the optimal decision. We present a monadic formulation of alpha-beta pruning based on the combination of the continuation monad and the reader monad. Unlike previous approaches that encode alpha-beta bounds into the types of available moves, our construction records these bounds within monadic outcomes, leaving the move types unchanged. We further show that the ordinary continuation monad suffices to compute not only optimal outcomes but also optimal plays, by extending the outcome type to include the corresponding sequences of moves. This provides an alternative to generalisations of the continuation monad proposed to address the inefficiencies associated with the selection monad in alpha-beta search. We illustrate our approach with an implementation of Tic-Tac-Toe, observing a 39-fold reduction in the number of plays evaluated, compared with exhaustive search, in computing an optimal play. Finally, we formally establish the correctness of our construction by proving that the monadic alpha-beta search computes the same optimal outcomes and plays as exhaustive minimax search. Our results demonstrate how a foundational algorithm in AI can be expressed and verified using standard monadic abstractions, providing a basis for further development of compositional approaches to adversarial search.
item.dc:creator: Mart\'in Escard\'o, Paulo Oliva

item.title: On the Effect of Bounded Rationality in Mixed Duopoly Markets
item.description: arXiv:2404.19236v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nash equilibrium is a common solution concept that captures strategic interaction in market analysis. However, it assumes that all market participants are fully rational and can compute mutually consistent best responses. Level-k reasoning relaxes this assumption by modeling bounded rationality through finite reasoning depth. In this paper, we consider a variation of Cournot competition that includes two suppliers, both following level-k reasoning. One is a self-interested firm and the other serves as a benevolent social planner. First, we show that social welfare is maximized when the planner is one level more rational than its opponent. Welfare is weakly decreasing as the planner's level moves away from this optimum. We then show that welfare under bounded rationality can differ substantially from welfare at Nash equilibrium. We characterize optimal, expectation-maximizing, and robust maximin strategies for the planner under different amounts of information about its opponent's rationality level. Finally, we show how utility design can improve social welfare by allowing the planner to cooperate with or fight the self-interested firm. Numerical experiments further demonstrate and validate our findings.
item.dc:creator: Lihui Yi, Ermin Wei

item.title: Playing Markov Games Without Observing Payoffs
item.description: arXiv:2509.00179v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimization under uncertainty is a fundamental problem in learning and decision-making, particularly in multi-agent systems. Previously, Feldman, Kalai, and Tennenholtz [2010] demonstrated the ability to efficiently compete in repeated symmetric two-player matrix games without observing payoffs, as long as the opponents actions are observed. In this paper, we introduce and formalize a new class of zero-sum symmetric Markov games, which extends the notion of symmetry from matrix games to the Markovian setting. We show that even without observing payoffs, a player who knows the transition dynamics and observes only the opponents sequence of actions can still compete against an adversary who may have complete knowledge of the game. We formalize three distinct notions of symmetry in this setting and show that, under these conditions, the learning problem can be reduced to an instance of online learning, enabling the player to asymptotically match the return of the opponent despite lacking payoff observations. Our algorithms apply to both matrix and Markov games, and run in polynomial time with respect to the size of the game and the number of episodes. Our work broadens the class of games in which robust learning is possible under severe informational disadvantage and deepens the connection between online learning and adversarial game theory.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Ablin, Alon Cohen

item.title: Scaling Chance-Constrained Correlated Equilibrium Computation for Exclusive Resource-Assignment Games
item.description: arXiv:2609.13565v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The chance-constrained correlated equilibrium concept provides a robust coordination technique for self-interested agents whose costs are uncertain to a central coordinator, but the number of joint actions considered in its computation grows exponentially with the number of agents. We develop a reduced-rank formulation based on convex combinations of chance-constrained pure Nash equilibria to improve scalability. To further reduce computation, we propose an exact-one resource-assignment restriction for games in which agents compete for shared resources and simultaneous use of a resource is undesirable or unsafe. The restriction allows each resource to be assigned to exactly one agent, reducing the number of joint actions considered from O(2^(nr)) to O(n^r) for n agents and r resources. The resulting problem is solved over the restricted joint action set while retaining all incentive constraints associated with unilateral deviations. We show that the feasible set of the restricted problem is exactly the convex hull of the chance-constrained pure Nash equilibria contained in the exact-one assignment set, yielding a necessary and sufficient condition for nonemptiness. We further derive a sufficient condition under which all chance-constrained pure Nash equilibria of the unrestricted game are retained by the restriction. Numerical experiments in a vertiport departure-corridor coordination scenario demonstrate a 99.81% reduction in median computation time relative to the unrestricted formulation while achieving equivalent coordination performance.
item.dc:creator: Jaehan Im, Ufuk Topcu, David Fridovich-Keil

item.title: From Reconnaissance to Response: Quantitative Risk Parameterization and Game Theoretic Containment in Modern Enterprise Attack
item.description: arXiv:2609.36485v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern Security Operations Centers struggle with delayed manual incident response, enabling adversaries to advance through the Cyber Kill Chain during early stage reconnaissance. While classical game theoretic defense models optimize strategic resource allocation, they rely on static utility matrices that fail to adapt to dynamic telemetry. This paper presents an integrated, metrics driven decision engine that bridges quantitative risk parameterization and continuous automated response time. Common Vulnerability Scoring Systems exploitability parameters are mapped to attacker success probabilities and evaluate defender log distributions via Factor Analysis of Information Risk Monte Carlo simulations. Real time SIEM logs streams are modeled as Poisson process arrival rates, dynamically updating defender posterior threat belief through sequential Bayesian filtering. A closed form threshold is derived by framing the interaction as a dynamic Bayesian Stackelberg game, where the expected unmitigated risk exceeds proactive containment cost. Parameterized against empirical data from the 2023 MGM Resorts and Caesars Entertainment cyber incident, simulation results demonstrate that the engine suppresses transient background noise while triggering automated SOAR network isolation within seconds of adversarial probing. Multi parameter sensitivity analysis confirms that the decision boundary dynamically adjusts to live perimeter vulnerability, offering a control theoretic foundation for sub minute automated threat containment.
item.dc:creator: Shadeeb Hossain, Elias Calboreanu

item.title: Why Last-Iterate Scale-Invariant Regret Matching Converges Linearly?
item.description: arXiv:2609.38162v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scale-invariant extragradient regret matching (IREG-PRM+) normalizes the cumulative regret vector by its own norm and attains optimal regret without knowing the payoff scale. On two-player zero-sum matrix games, its last iterate converges linearly in experiments. Prior theory leaves this behavior unexplained. Analysis is difficult because the algorithm lacks a fixed step size. The step size is the inverse of the regret norm, which changes along the trajectory. Existing proofs of linear rates for regret-matching dynamics rely on restarts or modified updates. We explain the unmodified algorithm's convergence through norm saturation. The regret norm grows to a finite limit, so the step size converges as well. We prove that saturation always occurs and provide an explicit upper bound. The last iterate then converges to a single Nash equilibrium in every two-player zero-sum matrix game, even with multiple equilibria. Near a unique equilibrium, the set of active actions freezes after one round, and the linearized dynamics have a closed form. Take the payoff matrix restricted to these active actions and centered by the game value. Whenever the limiting step size times this matrix's largest singular value is less than one, the last iterate converges linearly at a closed-form rate. Across $216$ random games, all $184$ instances with a numerically resolved limit satisfy this condition. The predicted rate matches the empirical rate with a median ratio of $1.000$. Our analysis also shows that the per-round increase in the squared regret norm scales with the squared Nash gap, which measures distance to equilibrium. In sequential games (extensive-form games), exact gap computation requires a costly best-response pass. On Kuhn and Leduc poker, the analogous norm increase tracks the Nash gap between infrequent passes. Our code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/NormCert
item.dc:creator: Boning Li, Longbo Huang

item.title: k-Submodular Cover Problem with a Matroid Constraint
item.description: arXiv:2610.26989v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate k-submodular cover problem with a matroid constraint on an n-element ground set V , which seeks k disjoint subsets of V with minimal cost, where their union is an independent set for some matroid defined on V and the k-submodular utility function surpasses a specified threshold. This problem generalizes the k-submodular cover problem and has a wide range of applications in artificial intelligence and combinatorial optimization. In this paper, we propose a matroid extended greedy algorithm for this problem, analyze its bi-criteria approximation ratio, and further derive an improved approximation ratio under the special case of unit costs.
item.dc:creator: Xinru Li, Donglei Du, Qian Liu, Yang Zhou, Min Li
